title: Received an IRS notice? What to do first
excerpt: Most IRS letters can be resolved calmly. Here's how to read the notice and respond the right way.
body:
Getting a letter from the IRS can be stressful, but many notices are routine — a request for information, a math correction or a balance reminder.

1. Don't ignore it

Every notice has a response deadline. Missing it can limit your options, so open the letter as soon as it arrives.

2. Identify the notice

Look for the notice number (for example "CP2000" or "CP14") in the top or bottom corner. It tells you what the IRS is asking for.

3. Compare with your return

Check the notice against the return it refers to. If the IRS is right, you can usually pay or agree. If not, you can respond with documentation.

4. Beware of scams

The IRS generally starts contact by mail. Be cautious of calls, texts or emails demanding immediate payment by gift card or wire transfer.

Not sure what your notice means? Send it to us and we'll explain your options during a free consultation.

title: How to check the status of your tax refund
excerpt: Federal and state refunds are tracked separately. Here's where to look and what you'll need.
body:
Your federal refund and your state refund are processed by different agencies, so you'll check each one separately.

What you'll need

  • Your Social Security number or ITIN

  • Your filing status

  • The exact refund amount shown on your return

Where to check

Use the official IRS refund tool for your federal refund, and your state's tax website for your state refund. You'll find direct links in the Resources section of this site.

If your refund is taking much longer than expected, or you received a letter about it, contact us and we'll help you find out why.

title: Why clean bookkeeping saves you money at tax time
excerpt: Organized books mean fewer missed deductions, faster filing and less stress if the IRS ever asks questions.
body:
Many small business owners only think about their books when tax season arrives. Keeping records up to date all year makes a real difference.

Fewer missed deductions

When expenses are recorded as they happen, legitimate business costs are less likely to be forgotten.

Better decisions

Current numbers show you cash flow, profit and where money is going — not just once a year.

Ready for questions

If you ever receive a notice or audit, organized records make it much easier to respond.

We offer bookkeeping and payroll support so you can focus on running your business.

title: Building a simple financial plan for your family
excerpt: A clear plan connects your taxes, savings, insurance and goals — and it doesn't have to be complicated.
body:
A good financial plan starts with your goals, not with products.

Start with the basics

  • Know what comes in and goes out each month

  • Build an emergency fund

  • Make sure your family is protected with the right insurance

Think about taxes

Your tax situation affects how much you keep. Planning ahead — not just at filing time — helps you avoid surprises.

Review regularly

Life changes such as marriage, a new child, a new job or starting a business are good moments to revisit your plan.

Want a second opinion on your plan? Schedule a complimentary consultation.
